value.overview: The Mangrove Vireo (Vireo pallens) is a small, mainly resident songbird of coastal Central America and southern Mexico. It is closely associated with mangrove forests, although it also uses nearby thorn scrub, overgrown fields, young secondary woodland, and forest edges. The species belongs to the vireo family, Vireonidae, and is often detected more readily by its repeated, somewhat harsh song than by direct views in dense coastal vegetation.
value.classification: The Mangrove Vireo is a passerine in the family Vireonidae and genus Vireo. Several geographic subspecies are recognized across its range, including forms occurring along the Pacific coast of Costa Rica.
value.identification: This is a small, compact vireo with olive-gray upperparts, a grayish head, pale underparts, yellowish areas around the face and sides, and two pale wing-bars. Its bill is fairly stout for its size. The eye pattern is less complete and less strongly marked than that of the White-eyed Vireo, helping distinguish the two where they overlap. In Costa Rica, its scratchy, repetitive chi-chi-chi song is a useful identification clue.
value.rangeHabitat: The Mangrove Vireo ranges from the Pacific and Caribbean coasts of southern Mexico through Central America, with additional populations on some Caribbean islands. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in coastal mangroves and associated lowland scrub, especially along the Pacific coast, including areas around the Gulf of Nicoya and other suitable coastal wetlands. It may also use adjacent dry woodland, brushy fields, young secondary growth, and forest edges, but is generally tied to lowland coastal habitats.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a sedentary, year-round resident rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, the species is present throughout the year in suitable Pacific-coast mangroves and nearby scrub; seasonal movements within the country are not well documented.
value.breeding: Information on breeding is limited. The few described nests were found in Belize during April–June and were small, deep cups made from plant fibers, bark, grasses, lichen, and spider web, placed low in a tree. Clutches contained two or three eggs. In Costa Rica, breeding likely occurs during the local wet-season breeding period, but detailed information on nesting dates, territory size, incubation, and parental care remains scarce.
value.dietFeeding: The Mangrove Vireo feeds primarily on insects and other small arthropods, including spiders, and also takes some fruit. It usually forages low or at middle levels in mangrove foliage and dense scrub, gleaning prey from leaves and small branches. Birds may forage alone or in pairs and sometimes join mixed-species feeding groups. Its deliberate movements and repeated pauses are typical of many vireos.
value.behavior: This species is generally inconspicuous and spends much of its time within dense vegetation. It moves through foliage with short hops and brief flights while searching methodically for prey. The song varies geographically; in Costa Rica it is described as a repetitive, scratchy series of notes. It is usually encountered singly or in pairs, although it may participate in mixed-species flocks outside the breeding season.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although it remains relatively widespread and is not currently considered globally threatened.
